Reverential means showing or expressing a feeling of very deep, humble respect mixed with a sense of awe — the kind of respect you feel not just in your mind, but that shows up in the way you speak, act, move, and carry yourself.

It goes well beyond ordinary, everyday respect. When your attitude is reverential, you are not just being polite or courteous. You feel that the person, place, or thing in front of you is so important, so great, so sacred, or so superior, that you naturally want to lower yourself in their presence — not physically always, but emotionally and mentally.

Think of the difference between these two scenarios:

  • You greet your neighbour. You smile, say hello, exchange a few casual words. That is being polite.
  • You are brought into the presence of someone you consider the greatest human being alive — a person who changed your life, or shaped the course of history. Suddenly your voice softens. You choose your words carefully. You feel almost unworthy to be there. That is being reverential.

The word captures that specific quality — a kind of quiet, deep, humble admiration that is almost solemn. There is often a sense of "I am small; this thing before me is great."
What Reverential Looks Like in Practice

Because it is an adjective, "reverential" usually describes either:

A person's attitude or behavior:

"He had a reverential attitude toward his grandfather."

This means he treated his grandfather with deep, almost sacred respect — not just obedience or affection, but genuine awe.

A tone, voice, or manner of speaking:

"She spoke about the painting in a reverential tone."

Her voice was hushed, careful, full of admiration — as though speaking too loudly would somehow disrespect the work.

A silence, atmosphere, or mood:

"A reverential silence fell over the crowd."

The kind of silence that descends naturally when people feel they are in the presence of something deeply significant. Think of the silence in a great cathedral, or the moment before a war memorial is unveiled.

A gaze or look:

"The students looked at their mentor with reverential eyes."

Their gaze was not just attentive — it was full of admiration and awe.

The thing that separates reverential from simply respectful is awe. Awe is that slightly overwhelming feeling that something is far bigger, greater, or more powerful than you. You can respect a good colleague. But you feel reverential toward something or someone that you consider truly extraordinary — a masterpiece, a great leader, a sacred place, an ancient text, or a force of nature.

Think of a person standing at the edge of the Grand Canyon for the first time. They go quiet. They may take off their hat. Their voice drops. They might say nothing at all for a moment. That is reverential behavior — brought on by something so vast and magnificent that ordinary behavior feels inappropriate.
Reverential vs. Reverent — Know the Difference

These two words are closely related and often confused, so let's clear this up.

  • Reverent describes a person's inner feeling or overall character. A reverent person is someone who naturally carries deep respect within them — "He was a reverent man."
  • Reverential describes the outward quality, tone, manner, or atmosphere that such feelings produce — "He spoke in a reverential whisper." "A reverential hush filled the room."

In short: reverent is what you are or feel, while reverential is what your behavior, voice, or manner looks like to the outside world. In practice, the two overlap heavily, and many writers use them interchangeably — but this distinction is worth knowing.

• It is not sycophancy (fake, exaggerated flattery for selfish purposes).
  • It is not blind obedience.
  • It is not fear, though it can sometimes contain a shade of it.
  • It is not casual admiration like saying, "Oh, I really like that band."

Reverential respect is genuine, deep, and often solemn. It is the opposite of being flippant, irreverent, or dismissive.

• Reverential awe — deep respect and wonder combined.
  • Reverential silence — a hush that comes from being in the presence of something great.
  • Reverential tone — a soft, careful, serious way of speaking.
  • Reverential attitude — an overall approach of humble, deep respect.
  • Reverential gaze — looking at something with awe and admiration.
  • Reverential treatment — handling or discussing something with extreme care and respect.

Reverential means showing a deep, humble, awe-filled respect toward someone or something considered extraordinary, sacred, or profoundly great — a respect so strong that it changes the way you speak, act, and carry yourself in their presence.
